originality.rationale: Gusev 2014 proves an expectation formula for a random input to the pair automaton and describes its odd-n transition graph; neither his graph lemma nor his expected-value theorem asserts the cost-independent unique shortest word for all pairs and parities, two separate letter-count lower bounds, or the exact distance spectrum. The graph supplies a useful prior technical ingredient, not a theorem already expressing these conclusions. Published generic shortest-reset and weighted-synchronization algorithms do not dominate the exact all-pair fixed-family theorem. Published research-record and primary-literature comparisons are evidence of no located coverage, not a general novelty certificate.
residual_risks: Gusev 2014 completely describes the odd-state pair graph; an unindexed prior source may already have extracted deterministic distances or Pareto-minimal paths from that graph.

The later weighted-approximation article supplies a general pair-state shortest-path algorithm and so the exact formula is algorithmically computable from known transitions; an unindexed older article may have derived the same cost result explicitly.
No claim of global historical uniqueness or independent verification is made.

value.rationale: The natural problem is exact pair synchronization under unequal operation costs, central to finite-automaton control. An explicit all-n classification and a single word optimizing both resource counts separately for every initial pair is stronger than a one-cost shortest-path table, especially because shortest paths need not be robust across costs in general automata. The bijection between all pairs and every shortest merging length 1..binomial(n,2) gives a rigid structural invariant and exact boundary behavior for even antipodal pairs. The result covers arbitrarily large n, with a mathematical proof, not merely an exhaustive finite experiment.
